# Law, Regulation, and Policy {#sec-law-policy}

Legal compliance is a dated claim about a specific system, its intended use, the actor performing that use, the jurisdiction, the effective date, and the source version on which the analysis relies. Change any element and the answer may change. A general-purpose model can be lawful in one product and prohibited in another; the same company can be a deployer in one transaction and a provider in the next.

Law is therefore an engineering input that shapes the design before launch. Market choice affects data rights, documentation, interface notices, human review, logging, incident clocks (the deadlines for reporting an incident), and whether a system may be offered at all. Those constraints reach into @sec-data-curation, @sec-model-artifacts, @sec-privacy-provenance, @sec-security-authorization, @sec-runtime-safety, @sec-operational-evaluation, and @sec-confidential-inference.

This chapter supplies an operational method for finding and preserving that claim. It is not legal advice. Counsel must interpret the law for the facts, but engineering must maintain the facts and evidence on which that interpretation depends.

## Start with source and status

Governance documents differ in legal force: some are law, while others are guidance, standards, contracts, or voluntary commitments. A useful legal register records the source type and its current status before extracting a requirement.

| Source | What it can do | Status questions to record |
|---|---|---|
| Enacted law | Creates obligations within its scope, subject to its application and transition rules | Is it in force, applicable, effective, and enforceable for this actor and use? |
| Binding agency rule or order | Implements authority delegated by law and may bind covered actors | Which agency, scope, exceptions, review path, and operative date apply? |
| Official guidance | Explains an authority's interpretation or enforcement posture | Is it nonbinding, current, final, or draft? Which text does it interpret? |
| Treaty | Binds its parties after the conditions for entry into force and domestic effect are met | Was it only signed, or also ratified? Is it in force for this party? |
| Consensus standard | Defines requirements or guidance developed by a standards body | Is it voluntary, certifiable, and incorporated into law or contract? |
| Voluntary framework or company policy | Organizes self-governance and public commitments | Who can revise it, who reviews it, and has a contract or statute incorporated it? |
| Contract | Allocates duties and remedies between its parties | Which version, territory, service, audit right, and precedence clause govern? |

Each status term names a different legal state. *Enacted* does not necessarily mean *effective*. *Signed* does not mean *ratified*. *Ratified* does not necessarily mean *in force*. A proposed bill, a voluntary code, official guidance, and an enforceable regulation can address the same control without sharing legal force. Preserve each source, publication date, version, and retrieval date rather than storing a paraphrase called “the AI rules.”

## Classify before mapping controls

Compliance starts from an inventory of the whole system, in which the model is one component. The workflow repeats on every deployment change, and such changes are common.

The workflow runs six steps in order:

1. Inventory the service, its data, decisions, users, affected people, and markets.
2. Identify every actor and its role in each supply chain.
3. Classify the system and intended use under both AI-specific and existing law.
4. Map horizontal and sectoral law, then check effective dates, transitions, and exceptions.
5. Map each obligation to a control and artifact, and assign an owner and reviewer.
6. Monitor changes in both the system and the governing sources.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-law-versioned-claim
//| fig-cap: "A compliance conclusion is valid only for the recorded system facts and legal sources. A change monitor watches both inputs; a change at either reopens classification, and the release claim is held until the obligations, controls, and evidence have been reviewed again."
digraph claim {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  graph [nodesep=0.3, ranksep=0.3];
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#374151", fillcolor="#f1ece1", margin="0.08,0.05"];
  facts [label="System facts\nuse · actor · market · revision"];
  monitor [label="Change monitor\nmodel swap · new use\nnew market · role change\nsource update"];
  sources [label="Legal sources\nstatus · version · effective date"];
  classify [label="Classification\nand obligation map", color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#2563eb"];
  evidence [label="Controls · evidence\nowners · reporting clocks"];
  release [label="Reviewed release claim"];
  edge [color="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.55, fontsize=9, fontcolor="#6b7280"];
  facts -> classify;
  sources -> classify;
  classify -> evidence -> release;
  facts -> monitor [style=dashed, label="change"];
  monitor -> sources [style=dashed, dir=back, label="change"];
  monitor -> classify [label="reopen"];
  monitor -> release [style=dashed, label="hold reuse"];
  {rank=same; facts; monitor; sources;}
}
```

## The EU AI Act: several parallel classifications

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is a horizontal AI law, but it does not sort every system into four mutually exclusive tiers. Its structure combines prohibited practices, high-risk classifications, transparency duties, and a parallel regime for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. Other Union and national law continues to apply [@euaiact2024].

### Scope and use-based duties

Article 2 reaches more than EU-established companies. It covers providers placing systems or general-purpose models on the Union market regardless of establishment, EU deployers, specified supply-chain actors, and some third-country providers or deployers where the output is used in the Union. That is direct statutory scope. The separate @gls-brussels-effect describes the economic choice to reuse an EU-oriented design elsewhere; it is not a substitute for the scope analysis [@bradford2020brussels].

The principal paths are:

- **Prohibited practices.** Article 5 defines practices that are barred when their statutory elements are met. Labels such as “social scoring” or “biometric identification” are only shorthand; the text includes conditions and exceptions that must be tested.
- **High-risk systems.** Article 6(1) covers certain safety components and products listed through Annex I when the specified product-law and conformity conditions apply. Article 6(2) and Annex III cover enumerated uses in areas including biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice. Article 6(3) provides a bounded route for some Annex III systems not to be high-risk; profiling systems do not receive that route. Not every high-risk assessment requires a third-party auditor.
- **Transparency.** Article 50 assigns different provider and deployer duties for direct interaction, machine-readable marking, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, deepfakes, and certain public-interest text. A single rule such as “label synthetic media” does not capture these duties, because the responsible actor, output type, disclosure mechanism, and exception differ from case to case.
- **General-purpose AI.** Chapter V applies at the model-provider layer in parallel with the classification of downstream systems. A downstream use can therefore add its own high-risk or transparency obligations.

High-risk providers must support risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, conformity assessment, registration, post-market monitoring, and incident handling where the corresponding provisions apply. Deployers have different duties, such as following instructions, assigning competent oversight, monitoring use, retaining controlled logs, and supporting affected-person or data-protection procedures. A fundamental-rights impact assessment is required only for the deployers and uses specified in Article 27, not for every high-risk deployment.

### General-purpose models and systemic risk

Article 53 requires a general-purpose AI provider to maintain technical documentation, give downstream providers information needed for integration, adopt a copyright-compliance policy, and publish a sufficiently detailed training-content summary. A provider outside the Union may also need an authorised representative. A qualifying open-source model can be exempt from parts of the technical-documentation and downstream-information duties, but not from the copyright policy or training-content summary; the exemption does not cover models with systemic risk [@eugpai2025].

Training compute above `10^25 FLOP` creates a rebuttable presumption of high-impact capability. A provider can submit a substantiated rebuttal, and the Commission may designate a model using the statutory criteria even when the presumption is not the route. Providers of general-purpose models with systemic risk must add model evaluation, documented adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, serious-incident reporting without undue delay, and cybersecurity for the model and its infrastructure [@euaiact2024; @eugpai2025].

### The current transition calendar

The date belongs in the classification record. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the enacted Digital Omnibus, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and changed the original schedule [@euomnibus2026].

| Date | Operational meaning |
|---|---|
| 2 February 2025 | The original prohibited-practice, scope, definition, and AI-literacy provisions began applying. |
| 2 August 2025 | The general-purpose AI duties and specified governance and penalty provisions began applying. |
| 2 August 2026 | Most remaining provisions apply, including most Article 50 duties; Commission enforcement and fines for GPAI providers begin. |
| 2 December 2026 | New prohibited practices added by the Omnibus apply; a transition for specified legacy output-marking systems ends. |
| 2 August 2027 | General-purpose models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply. |
| 2 December 2027 | Chapter III Sections 1–3 apply to Article 6(2), Annex III high-risk systems. |
| 2 August 2028 | Those sections apply to Article 6(1), Annex I product-related high-risk systems. |
| 2 August 2030 | High-risk systems intended for use by public authorities that were placed on the market before the Chapter III dates must comply, whether or not their design has changed significantly. |

This table is a snapshot at the chapter's review date, and later acts can change it again. Preserve the authentic acts and the consolidated text used for analysis. The Omnibus itself demonstrates why a launch checklist cannot hard-code a date and then stop monitoring it.

## Roles move along the value chain

An organization can occupy several roles at once. Record the role per system, market, and transaction.

| Role | Operational question |
|---|---|
| Provider | Who develops or has the system developed and places it on the market or puts it into service under its name or trademark? |
| GPAI provider | Who develops or has the general-purpose model developed and places that model on the market? |
| Downstream provider | Who integrates a general-purpose model into another model or system and needs upstream evidence? |
| Deployer | Who uses the system under its authority, outside purely personal non-professional use? |
| Importer | Which EU-established actor first places a third-country-branded system on the Union market? |
| Distributor | Which other supply-chain actor makes the system available? |
| Product manufacturer | Who places a covered product on the market with an AI system under its own name or trademark? |
| Authorised representative | Which EU-established person holds a written mandate for a non-EU provider? |

Role can change by action. Under Article 25, rebranding, a substantial modification, or changing the intended purpose so that a system becomes high-risk can make an importer, distributor, deployer, or third party the provider. A procurement contract can allocate evidence and cooperation, but it cannot erase a statutory role.

This is why vendor review cannot end with “the model is compliant.” Ask which legal entity made which claim, for which revision and intended purpose, and whether the integration changes the role or classification.

## The United States: overlapping authorities

The United States has no single comprehensive horizontal federal AI statute for private systems as of this chapter's review date. That does not create a legal vacuum. Consumer protection, anti-discrimination, employment, credit, privacy, health, product safety, intellectual property, contract, and other sectoral rules can govern an AI-mediated act just as they govern the same act performed with other software.

Federal documents also differ in reach. OMB Memorandum M-25-21 governs covered federal agencies' own use of AI and expressly does not create rights or obligations for the public. M-25-22 governs covered federal acquisition; its requirements can reach a vendor through procurement and contract terms, not as a general private-market AI statute [@omb2025m2521; @omb2025m2522]. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and Generative AI Profile organize voluntary risk work into Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. They are not laws or NIST certifications. Selected controls become binding only when a law, regulation, order, or contract incorporates them [@nist2023airmf; @nist2024genai].

State law must be read actor by actor and date by date:

| Jurisdiction | Binding example | Scope and operative date |
|---|---|---|
| Colorado | SB 26-189 | Repeals and reenacts the earlier regime, SB 24-205, whose requirements a 2025 act had postponed to 30 June 2026 [@colorado2025sb25b004]; signed 14 May 2026, before that date. Most provisions take effect 1 January 2027 and apply to consequential decisions made on or after that date. Developers and deployers of covered automated decision-making technology have different documentation, notice, review, and record duties. The attorney general enforces the act as a deceptive trade practice and, where a cure is possible, must offer a 60-day cure period before actions brought before 1 January 2030; the act creates no new private right of action [@colorado2026sb189]. |
| California | SB 53, Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act | Effective 1 January 2026. A frontier model uses more than `10^26` training operations. All covered frontier developers have specified transparency, incident-reporting, and whistleblower duties; the annual frontier-framework and fuller risk duties apply to a large frontier developer, defined in part by more than $500 million in prior-year gross revenue with affiliates [@casb53]. |
| California | SB 1119, companion chatbots and children's safety | Chapter 190, Statutes of 2026. From 1 July 2027, an operator must perform and document a risk assessment for minor users before making a new or substantially modified companion chatbot available, and must obtain an independent child-safety audit by 1 January 2029 or before first public availability, whichever is later. Civil penalties reach $5,000 per affected child for each negligent violation and $15,000 for each intentional one, and a harmed child or parent may sue [@casb1119]. |
| California | AB 1405, AI auditor registration | Chapter 178, Statutes of 2026. The Government Operations Agency must open an AI Auditor Registry by 1 January 2029. From that date an unregistered person may not offer, sell, or conduct a covered AI audit, an audit of the controls an AI system or model needs to comply with state law [@caab1405]. |
| New York | RAISE Act as amended | Effective 1 January 2027. Its frontier and large-developer thresholds resemble California's, and an office within the Department of Financial Services receives its reports, but registration, assessment, disclosure, and incident rules must be read from New York's own text [@nyraise2026]. |

These examples do not form a universal US tier system. The California and New York incident clocks, Colorado's adverse-outcome review, a California audit-registration rule, an Illinois employer's use restriction, and a federal procurement clause attach to different events and actors.

Federal preemption, an effort to have federal law override state rules, is being pursued through executive instruments whose legal force differs from one to the next. Executive Order 14365 directs agencies to act against state AI laws that conflict with a national policy, and states that it creates no right or benefit enforceable at law [@whitehouse2025eo14365]. A separate order, EO 14409, sets up a voluntary pre-release channel for models with advanced cyber capability [@whitehouse2026eo14409]. Each instrument needs its own status entry:

| Instrument | What it does | Legal force to record |
|---|---|---|
| EO 14365, section 3 | The Attorney General forms an AI Litigation Task Force whose sole responsibility is to challenge state AI laws in court. | Litigation: a state law's status changes only if a court rules against it. |
| EO 14365, sections 4 and 5 | Commerce publishes an evaluation naming “onerous” state AI laws; states that keep them become ineligible for remaining broadband (BEAD) non-deployment funds to the maximum extent federal law allows. | A condition on a state's federal funding, with no duty on a developer. |
| EO 14365, section 6 | The Federal Communications Commission opens a proceeding to decide whether to adopt a federal reporting and disclosure standard for AI models that preempts conflicting state laws. | None until the Commission adopts a rule. |
| EO 14365, section 7, and the FTC proposal | The Federal Trade Commission proposed a policy statement on deception under section 5 of the FTC Act. It names Colorado's revised act as a state law whose compliance could lead a company to steer outputs deceptively, and argues that conflicting state law is impliedly preempted [@ftc2026accuracy]. | A proposed enforcement policy statement: the Commission's reading of section 5, not a rule and not a court ruling on any state statute. |
| EO 14365, section 8 | A legislative recommendation for a preemptive federal framework that would leave state laws on child safety, AI compute and data-center infrastructure, and state procurement and use of AI in place. | None unless Congress enacts it. |
| EO 14409, section 3 | A classified benchmark, with the determination made by the Director of the National Security Agency, designates “covered frontier models” by cyber capability; a voluntary framework lets developers give the government access to such a model for up to 30 days before releasing it to other trusted partners. | Voluntary for developers; the order states that it authorizes no mandatory licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement. |

An executive order or an agency policy statement is therefore not itself a judgment that a given state rule is invalid. The register records the instrument, its stage, and the state rule it targets, and keeps the state duty mapped until a court, a statute, or an adopted rule changes its status.

::: {.callout-note .dated}

EO 14365 was signed on 11 December 2025 and EO 14409 on 2 June 2026 [@whitehouse2025eo14365; @whitehouse2026eo14409]. The FTC published its proposal on 7 July 2026 with comments due by 31 July 2026, and no final statement had appeared in the Federal Register as of 22 September 2026 [@ftc2026accuracy].

## International instruments and standards

The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law is a treaty designed to bind parties after entry into force. It was opened for signature in 2024 and enters into force only after five ratifications, at least three of them by Council of Europe member states. Its status must therefore be recorded as signed or ratified per participant, not as universally enforceable current law [@coe2024framework].

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

The treaty office's chart dated 23 September 2026 lists one ratification, by the European Union on 15 May 2026, and 20 signatures not followed by ratification. The convention is not yet in force [@coe2024framework].
:::

The OECD AI Principles are a non-legally-binding Council Recommendation. They offer a shared vocabulary for human rights, transparency, robustness, safety, traceability, and lifecycle risk management; they do not certify a product or create a reporting mandate by themselves [@oecd2024principles].

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 specifies requirements for an organizational AI management system. An organization can obtain third-party certification of a defined management-system scope against it. ISO itself does not certify organizations, and the certificate is not a finding that a particular model is safe, correct, or legally compliant. The standard is voluntary unless incorporated into law or contract [@iso420012023]. A crosswalk, a table that maps one framework's clauses onto another's, shows correspondence, not equivalence.

These distinctions produce two independent axes:

- **Legal force:** enacted law, binding rule, treaty in force, contract, guidance, standard, or voluntary policy.
- **Assurance object:** organizational management system, system classification, model evaluation, data right, incident process, or a particular legal requirement.

A strong audit of a management system can still say little about a specific model's behavior. A strong behavioral evaluation can still omit data rights. Neither becomes a legal opinion merely because it is independent.

## Existing law still governs the system

AI-specific law adds to rather than replaces existing duties. A legal map should include at least:

- **Data protection and privacy.** The GDPR can govern collection, training, inference, profiling, data-subject rights, security, impact assessment, retention, deletion, and personal-data-breach reporting. Its Article 33 72-hour breach clock is distinct from an AI safety-incident clock [@gdpr2016]. The data inventory and deletion evidence therefore belong with @sec-privacy-provenance.
- **Consumer protection.** Deceptive capability, disclosure, price, endorsement, or safety claims can matter even when no AI-specific tier applies.
- **Employment and credit.** Anti-discrimination, notice, accuracy, explanation, and review rules can attach to the decision and the deployer, not merely to the upstream model.
- **Product safety and liability.** An AI component can inherit sector-specific obligations and evidence from the product into which it is integrated.
- **Intellectual property and contract.** Copyright, database rights, licenses, terms, confidentiality, and trade-secret controls affect corpus acquisition, output use, model access, and evidence sharing.

### Copyright does not have one global answer

Training and corpus acquisition must be analyzed separately by jurisdiction, source, license, use, and procedural posture. In the United States, 2025 district-court decisions illustrate the limits of generalization. *Bartz v. Anthropic* treated the training use before it as fair use while separating acquisition and retention of pirated copies. *Kadrey v. Meta* granted summary judgment on the record presented and emphasized the plaintiffs' failure to establish the relevant market harm. *Thomson Reuters v. Ross* rejected fair use for a different, non-generative system competing in a legal-research market [@bartz2025order; @kadrey2025order; @ross2025].

Those decisions are jurisdiction-specific, fact-specific, and tied to procedural posture. They do not settle whether all training is fair use, whether a particular corpus was lawfully acquired, or how another country's exceptions apply. A settlement does not create precedent. The engineering response is provenance: retain source, acquisition method, license or exception analysis, rights-reservation signal, transformations, exclusions, deletion path, and model revision. “Publicly accessible” is not a license.

In the EU, the AI Act's GPAI copyright-policy and training-content-summary duties coexist with copyright law; they do not decide whether every included work was lawful. The summary is not necessarily a public row-by-row corpus manifest. Technical controls should implement the actual legal interpretation, including rights reservations where applicable, rather than inventing a universal opt-out rule.

## Voluntary frontier policies: useful, revisable, and bounded

Frontier developers publish policies that link a capability threshold to an evaluation, a safeguard tier, and sometimes a safety case. These structures can make release reasoning explicit and can be incorporated into a statute or contract. California SB 53, for example, requires a covered large frontier developer to publish, implement, and update a frontier AI framework [@casb53].

The underlying company documents remain voluntary self-governance except where a binding source incorporates a duty. A company policy can be revised by its author, internal leadership may retain the launch decision, and public evaluators may receive only time-bounded access. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework are therefore evidence systems that can be compared with one another, and none has legal force of its own [@anthropic2026rsp34; @openai2025preparedness; @deepmind2026fsf31].

The document a statute reaches can be a different one. SB 53 obliges the developer to comply with the framework it publishes [@casb53], and Anthropic and OpenAI have each published a document for that purpose that is separate from their voluntary policy. Anthropic published a Frontier Compliance Framework in December 2025 as its compliance framework “for SB 53 and other regulatory requirements” and said that “the RSP will remain our voluntary safety policy” [@anthropic2025fcf]. The RSP itself states that where laws such as SB 53 define terms with specific thresholds, Anthropic addresses those requirements “in separate compliance frameworks” [@anthropic2026rsp34]. OpenAI's Frontier Governance Framework, published in May 2026, explains how its practices align with SB 53 and with the EU AI Act's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI, while “the Preparedness Framework remains the foundation” [@openai2026fgf]. The statutory duty to comply therefore attaches to the compliance framework. The voluntary policy stays revisable by its author and, in Anthropic's words, can go beyond or otherwise differ from current regulatory requirements. A legal register records both documents, the version of each in force at a given determination, and the points where they diverge.

The common pattern is still useful:

1. Define the harm pathway and capability threshold before the release decision.
2. Run an evaluation designed to elicit the capability under stated access and scaffolding.
3. Apply deployment and security safeguards when the threshold or uncertainty rule fires.
4. Write a safety case that connects evidence, assumptions, residual risk, and approval.
5. Preserve deviations, policy versions, reviewers, and the final decision.

The policy is evidence about governance. By itself it does not show that the threshold is complete, the evaluation elicited every capability, the safeguards will generalize, or the residual risk is acceptable.

### Thresholds for automated AI research

Most thresholds in these frameworks describe help a model could give an attacker, such as meaningful assistance toward a biological weapon or a cyberattack. The thresholds for automated AI research describe the model's effect on the developer itself: how fast it can produce the next, more capable model. That risk can arise inside the developer before any external release, so the response has to cover internal use and further training as well as deployment. The evidence also comes largely from the developer's own records of research output and progress, which outsiders cannot inspect. Google DeepMind's framework states that it may use information about its own progress in accelerating machine-learning research, in addition to evaluations, to assess these levels [@deepmind2026fsf31].

The frameworks test for this risk in two ways. A substitution test asks whether models could do the work of the developer's research staff at comparable cost. An acceleration test asks whether the measured pace of AI progress has risen because of AI's contribution to research. The responses they attach are mostly security measures, several of them stated as levels from RAND's framework for protecting model weights, in which each higher level is meant to hold against a more capable attacker. The table sets out each framework's terms; the versions it reads are listed after it.

| Framework and threshold | Substitution or automation test | Acceleration test | Response the framework attaches |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anthropic RSP, automated R&D in key domains (evaluated on AI research for now) | Models could fully substitute for the company's entire set of research scientists and research engineers at competitive cost, within a factor of 5 | Double the rate of progress in aggregate AI capabilities, observed or expected, meaning as much progress in one year as in two at baseline, over at least three model generations and plausibly attributable to automated research or engineering | A company plan (security research, logging and AI review of all critical AI-development activity, systematic alignment assessments) and an industry-wide recommendation of security roughly at RAND security level 4, with controls that restrict even the most privileged insiders, up to the chief executive [@anthropic2026rsp34] |
| OpenAI Preparedness Framework, AI self-improvement | High: an impact equivalent to giving every OpenAI researcher a highly performant mid-career research engineer assistant, relative to a 2024 baseline. Critical, leading indicator: a superhuman research-scientist agent | Critical, lagging indicator: a generational model improvement, such as o1 to o3, in one fifth of the 2024 wall-clock time, sustained for several months | High: security controls meeting the High standard. Critical: “Until we have specified safeguards and security controls that would meet a Critical standard, halt further development” [@openai2025preparedness] |
| Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework, machine-learning R&D critical capability levels | Automation level 1: can fully automate the work of any Google team of researchers focused on improving AI capabilities, at approximately comparable all-inclusive cost | Acceleration level 1: has been used to accelerate AI development, with AI progress substantially accelerating from historical rates | Recommended security level 3 for acceleration and level 4 for automation, the latter to be “taken on by the frontier AI field as a whole”; deployment mitigations for external and high-risk internal deployments; a safety case once a level is reached [@deepmind2026fsf31] |

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

The table reads the versions each developer listed as current on 23 September 2026: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy version 3.4, effective 8 July 2026; OpenAI's Preparedness Framework version 2, updated 15 April 2025; and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework version 3.1, published 17 April 2026 [@anthropic2026rsp34; @openai2025preparedness; @deepmind2026fsf31]. OpenAI stated on 18 August 2026 that it will evolve its Preparedness Framework [@openai2026pacing].
:::

The two kinds of test fail differently. An acceleration test on observed progress is a lagging indicator: it fires after the acceleration it guards against has begun. Anthropic's version also counts expected acceleration, and OpenAI pairs its lagging indicator with a leading one, a superhuman research agent, so that the threshold can fire before the pace changes. A substitution test can fire earlier, but its result depends on how the developer measures its own staff's work and what it counts as comparable cost. Both tests rest on measurements the developer makes of itself, so the evidence used and the threshold text applied belong in the release record.

The response column is also text that its author revises and interprets. Anthropic's changelog records revisions to the automated R&D threshold in versions 3.1 and 3.4 of its policy, and says the threshold “has proven difficult to operationalize” [@anthropic2026rsp34]. OpenAI's Critical response makes resuming development conditional on safeguards that OpenAI itself specifies, and the framework sends every recommendation of its Safety Advisory Group to OpenAI leadership for the final decision [@openai2025preparedness]. A register that cites one of these policies should record the version in force at each determination, the clause applied, and who decided that its condition was met.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

GPT-6 Astra, released on 3 September 2026, is the first model OpenAI rated Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework. The system card rates it High in biological and chemical capability and below High in AI self-improvement [@openai2026astra]. For Critical cybersecurity capability, version 2 of the framework reads “Until we have specified safeguards and security controls standards that would meet a Critical standard, halt further development”, and it says OpenAI expected to update the framework before any model reached a Critical level [@openai2025preparedness]. On 7 August 2026 OpenAI concluded that it could not rule out Critical capability for Astra and paused internal Astra activities that did not yet meet strengthened security controls [@openai2026criticalcyber]. On 18 August it reported that, after the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and the Astra finding, it had paused reinforcement learning for two weeks on models intended for deployment and was holding its largest planned frontier training run [@openai2026pacing]. On 1 September it stated that Astra meets the Critical threshold, that it had restarted the large frontier run on 28 August once new safety and security requirements were in place, and that Astra's safeguards sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm for release [@openai2026pathastra]. The system card records the Safety Advisory Group's recommendation and leadership's determination that the safeguards suffice for public launch, and it links version 2 of the framework [@openai2026astra].
:::

## Turn requirements into evidence

Model cards and datasheets are valuable documentation patterns [@mitchell2019modelcards; @gebru2021datasheets]. They are not automatically the technical documentation, conformity assessment, impact assessment, post-market monitoring plan, or incident report required by a particular law. Reuse content, but do not treat artifact names as interchangeable.

The traceability chain should be explicit:

```text
source provision and version
  -> applicability and classification rationale
  -> requirement and responsible actor
  -> technical or organizational control
  -> artifact and system revision
  -> reviewer, approval, retention, and authority access
  -> monitoring trigger and reporting clock
```

One control can support several requirements, and one requirement can need several controls. The map must preserve that many-to-many relationship. It should also record negative evidence: an exception relied upon, missing vendor evidence, an unresolved legal conflict, or a control that does not cover a new modality.

Reporting clocks differ by regime, reporter, and recipient, so incident routing has its own table:

| Event | Possible regime | Reporter and recipient | Clock to verify |
|---|---|---|---|
| Personal-data breach | GDPR Article 33 | Controller to supervisory authority | Normally no later than 72 hours after awareness, subject to the statutory conditions [@gdpr2016] |
| High-risk-system serious incident | EU AI Act Article 73 | Covered provider to market-surveillance authorities | Event-specific deadlines, including shorter paths for specified harms [@euaiact2024] |
| GPAI systemic-risk serious incident | EU AI Act Article 55 | GPAI provider to the AI Office and relevant national authorities | Without undue delay [@euaiact2024] |
| California frontier critical safety incident | California SB 53 | Frontier developer to the state mechanism or appropriate authority | 15 days after discovery; 24 hours for specified imminent injury risk [@casb53] |
| New York frontier critical safety incident | New York RAISE Act as amended (S.8828) | Frontier developer to the office within the Department of Financial Services; imminent-risk disclosure to an appropriate authority, such as a law enforcement or public safety agency | 72 hours from determining that an incident occurred, or from learning facts sufficient for a reasonable belief that one did; 24 hours for imminent risk of death or serious physical injury [@nyraise2026] |

An event can trigger more than one row. The same critical safety incident runs on a 15-day clock in California and a 72-hour clock in New York, and the New York clock can start from a reasonable belief before any formal determination. The incident service should route by facts and jurisdiction, preserve awareness, discovery, and determination timestamps, and let the legal owner decide which clocks apply.

```{figure}
//| figure: incident-clocks
//| label: fig-law-incident-clocks
//| fig-cap: "One incident run through the numeric clocks of the table above, for a developer covered by both state laws and a controller under the GDPR. Time runs from discovery, and awareness of a personal-data breach is taken to be the same moment. The New York clock starts at the earlier of the reasonable belief and the formal determination, and each 24-hour imminent-risk path starts where its row's main clock starts; one toggle turns on both 24-hour paths, although their statutory conditions differ. Set the belief and the determination apart to see a New York deadline pass before any formal determination; an incident before the act takes effect on 1 January 2027 has no New York clock. The figure applies the table and is not legal advice."
```

### The legal register

Keep the register under version control and bind it to the release record:

```yaml
legal_register:
  system_and_model_revisions: []
  intended_purpose_and_prohibited_uses: []
  markets_jurisdictions_and_effective_dates: []
  actors_roles_and_contractual_allocation: []
  legal_sources_status_and_versions: []
  classification_and_risk_category: []
  sectoral_and_horizontal_obligations: []
  data_sources_rights_and_retention: []
  required_controls_and_evidence: []
  assessment_registration_and_authority_contacts: []
  transparency_human_oversight_and_appeal: []
  monitoring_incident_and_reporting_clocks: []
  change_triggers_and_reclassification: []
  exceptions_conflicts_and_legal_owner: []
  last_review_next_review_and_approver: []
```

Store source snapshots or stable identifiers alongside the register. A dashboard that says “EU AI Act: green” without article, actor, use, date, evidence, and revision does not say which requirement a given system revision meets.

### Regression scenarios

Treat compliance controls like other production controls. Re-run classification and evidence checks for at least these cases:

- **Market expansion:** an existing service becomes available in a new jurisdiction.
- **Role change:** a reseller rebrands the system, or an integrator makes a substantial modification.
- **Model swap:** the serving alias moves to a new base model or provider without updating evidence.
- **New intended use:** a general assistant is integrated into employment, credit, education, health, or public-service decisions.
- **GPAI designation:** a model crosses the compute presumption or receives a Commission designation.
- **Open-source condition:** license, distribution, monetization, or systemic-risk status invalidates an assumed exemption.
- **Stale guidance:** a control still cites withdrawn or superseded official guidance.
- **Deadline transition:** a provision becomes effective while the deployed revision remains unchanged.
- **Withdrawn standard:** certification or a contract still names an obsolete or withdrawn standard version.
- **Incident clock:** one event triggers privacy, AI safety, contractual, and sectoral reporting paths with different start times.
- **Authority request:** the organization must retrieve the exact logs, documentation, and unredacted evidence within scope.
- **Retention conflict:** an audit or litigation hold conflicts with a deletion request or minimization schedule.
- **Transparency label:** post-processing strips a machine-readable mark or required user notice.
- **Human-oversight bypass:** a product update removes the review or appeal path assumed by classification.
- **Vendor evidence:** an upstream provider stops supplying a required document or changes its contractual allocation.
- **Jurisdiction conflict:** one market requires disclosure that another contract or law restricts.

Every scenario should identify the detecting control, blocking behavior, evidence produced, escalation owner, and reapproval path. A warning with no release effect is not a regression test.

## What's contested

Several boundaries remain unsettled, and the register should say so rather than converting uncertainty into a categorical answer.

- **Which systems should bear fixed compliance costs?** Broad documentation and assessment duties can improve accountability while favoring organizations able to absorb them. Scope exceptions can protect small actors while leaving consequential uses under-governed.
- **Can compute stand in for capability?** A compute threshold is observable but indirect. Algorithmic efficiency, fine-tuning, tool access, and system composition can move risk without moving the original training number in the same way.
- **How much transparency is safe?** Regulators and downstream providers need evidence, while public disclosure can expose personal data, trade secrets, security controls, or dangerous capability details. Redaction and regulator-access rules mediate rather than eliminate the conflict.
- **What should independent assurance mean?** Access, sampling, standard, competence, conflicts, remediation authority, and publication all affect the strength of an audit. Independence alone does not make a narrow test comprehensive. California's AB 1405 turns one part of the question, who may conduct an audit used for state-law compliance, into a registration requirement from 2029 [@caab1405].
- **Who controls an open-weight system?** Upstream documentation can travel with weights, but downstream fine-tuning, repackaging, and deployment can change intended purpose, safeguards, and legal role beyond the original provider's observation.
- **When does copyright doctrine stabilize?** Outcomes may continue to differ by jurisdiction, acquisition method, market evidence, modality, and remedy. Product design must preserve options while courts and legislatures resolve those questions.

## Lower-layer constraint

Law reaches every lower layer through concrete design requirements. A data-rights analysis changes corpus admission and deletion in @sec-data-curation and @sec-privacy-provenance. Technical-documentation duties require lineage from @sec-model-artifacts. Human oversight and appeal require product and authorization paths from @sec-security-authorization. Transparency and incident duties add runtime metadata, logging, and routing to @sec-runtime-safety and @sec-operational-evaluation. Confidentiality limits affect which evidence can leave the boundary described in @sec-confidential-inference. Retention and regulator-access duties change storage, backup, and retrieval in @sec-orchestration-data-infra.

These constraints also have cost and latency consequences. A required review path, provenance mark, log, conformity process, or market-specific deployment adds work. @sec-economics must price that work, but cost does not decide whether an applicable duty can be ignored.

## Compliance must survive system change

A compliance memo describes a moment. A compliant operation maintains a chain from current facts and authoritative sources to classification, controls, evidence, review, monitoring, and reclassification. It also records which claims are legal conclusions, which are official guidance, which are standards, and which are voluntary promises.

No system is “compliant” in the abstract. A named organization has evidence that a named revision, used for a named purpose in a named jurisdiction on a named date, satisfies identified requirements under identified sources. When any name or date changes, the claim reopens.
